THOUGHT: The lesions arose 1–2 months after tattooing and are confined to the pink zones created by layering white ink (titanium dioxide) over red ink, strongly implicating a tattoo pigment–driven reaction. Histology shows epidermal and adnexal hyperplasia with granulomatous inflammation and abundant tattoo pigment in the dermis, without cytologic atypia or atypical keratinocyte nests, and tissue cultures were negative. Scanning electron/EDX confirms titanium dioxide (white) and red pigment in the affected dermis. These features favor a foreign-body/granulomatous reaction to tattoo ink (often to red pigment and to white titanium dioxide), commonly producing verrucous pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia that can clinically mimic infection or squamous cell carcinoma. Negative cultures argue against bacterial/fungal infection (including atypical mycobacteria), and lack of atypia argues against true squamous cell carcinoma, though both remain considerations clinically.

DIAGNOSIS:
1. Foreign-body granulomatous (granulomatous tattoo) reaction with pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia to tattoo pigment (red ink and titanium dioxide)
2. Delayed-type hypersensitivity / allergic granulomatous reaction to red/white tattoo pigments
3. Cutaneous atypical mycobacterial infection (e.g., Mycobacterium chelonae/abscessus) — post-tattoo infection (less likely given negative cultures and biopsy)
4. Sarcoidal granulomatous reaction localized to tattoo (sarcoidosis manifesting in tattooed skin)
5. Pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia mimicking squamous cell carcinoma (verrucous SCC) arising in tattoo (least likely given absence of cytologic atypia)

Case Information:
A black woman in her 50s presented with a 3-month history of nontender mildly pruritic verrucous nodules in several areas of a polychromatic tattoo on her right lower leg and foot. The nodules appeared 1-2 months following tattoo placement and were restricted to areas where pink zones were created by layering white ink over red ink. She denied pain, fevers, and chills. Past medical history included distant history of discoid lupus. She was taking 2 antihypertensives but no other oral or topical medications.

Physical Examination:
Well-demarcated erythematous to violaceous verrucous nodules on the right lateral leg and dorsal foot.
